{{Short description|British energy conversion expert (1932–2025)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2026}}
{{Use British English|date=January 2026}}
'''Ian Fells''', {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|CBE|FREng|FRSE}} (5 September 1932 – 20 August 2025) was a British energy conversion expert and academic. He was Professor of Energy Conversion at the [[University of Newcastle upon Tyne]], and chairman of the "New and Renewable Energy Centre" at [[Blyth, Northumberland]], England.

==Life and career==
Fells was born in [[Sheffield]], England on 5 September 1932.<ref name="obit">{{cite news |title=Professor Ian Fells obituary: scientist who won over Thatcher |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/obituaries/article/professor-ian-fells-obituary-scientist-who-won-over-thatcher-zlc26whvn |access-date=17 September 2025 |publisher=The Times |date=17 September 2025}}</ref> He was educated at [[King Edward VII School (Sheffield)|King Edward VII School]], [[Broomhill (ward)|Broomhill]], [[Sheffield]], then carried out [[national service]] in the [[British army]], before studying at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]] where he gained an [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] then in 1958 a [[PhD]] entitled "The kinetics of the hydrolysis of the chlorinated methanes".<ref name=CamLib>[http://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/ Cambridge University] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130615103726/http://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/ |date=15 June 2013 }} Newton Library catalogue</ref>
After lecturing in Chemical Engineering and Fuel Technology at the [[University of Sheffield]] he was appointed Reader in Fuel Science at King's College of [[Durham University|University of Durham]] in 1962. In 1963, this college became the [[University of Newcastle upon Tyne]], and he was on the staff of the [[Chemical Engineering]] Department.<ref name=Arches>[http://www.ncl.ac.uk/alumni/assets/documents/UtASpring08.pdf Underneath the Arches Spring 2008] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120222035208/http://www.ncl.ac.uk/alumni/assets/documents/UtASpring08.pdf |date=22 February 2012 }} The Fells Swoop (on Newcastle)</ref> He was Professor of Energy Conversion at Newcastle University from 1975 and published some 200 [[scientific publication|papers]] on a varied range of topics, including:

*The chemical physics of [[combustion]]
*[[fuel cell]]s
*[[rocket|rocket combustion]]
*[[energy economics]]
*[[environmental protection]]
*[[energy conversion]] systems
*[[energy policy]]

Fells was a long-standing advocate of [[nuclear power]].<ref name=gazettelive-20150709>{{cite news |url=https://www.gazettelive.co.uk/business/business-news/hartlepool-project-drive-down-cost-9622998 |title=Hartlepool project to drive down cost of UK's new nuclear fleet could be a world-first |newspaper=GazetteLive |location=Newcastle upon Tyne |date=9 July 2015 |accessdate=27 June 2018}}</ref> As of 2008, Fells was of the view that "any notion that renewables can provide for all our [energy] requirements is a mischievous and reckless boast".<ref name=guardian-20080918>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2008/sep/18/cleantechnology100 |title=We need an expensive miracle |last=Fells |first=Ian |newspaper=The Guardian |date=18 September 2008 |accessdate=27 June 2018}}</ref>

Fells made over 500 television and radio programmes, including the popular TV science series ''Take Nobody's Word For It'' with [[Carol Vorderman]], and regularly appeared as a guest expert and judge on ''[[The Great Egg Race]]'' from 1979 to 1986.<ref name=BBCnews>[https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/794078.stm "Scientists honoured across the UK"], ''BBC News'', 16 June 2000</ref><ref name=GENOME>{{cite web |title=BBC Genome Programme Index |url=https://genome.ch.bbc.co.uk/search/0/20?order=first&q=%40title+%22The+Great+Egg+Race%22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240327210749/https://genome.ch.bbc.co.uk/search/0/20?order=first&q=@title+%22The+Great+Egg+Race%22 |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 March 2024 |website=BBC Genome Project |publisher=BBC |access-date=27 March 2024}}</ref>

He was a science adviser to the [[World Energy Council]] and a special adviser to select committees of both the [[House of Lords]] and the [[British House of Commons|House of Commons]] as well as serving on several Cabinet and Research Council committees. He was chairman of the UK-based [[National Renewable Energy Centre (Narec)]],<ref>[http://www.nr.titech.ac.jp/coe21/eng/events/ines1/pdf/58_omoto.pdf IAEA: ''NUCLEAR POWER Current, Future Prospect and The Agency's Activities''] 1 November 2004</ref> was an energy adviser to the [[European Union]] and [[European Parliament]], advised a number of Foreign Governments on energy policy; and was a consultant to various multinational companies.

In 2012, he joined Newcastle-based company Penultimate Power UK as the Technical Director to develop [[small modular reactor]]s.<ref name=gazettelive-20150709/><ref name=chroniclelive-20160210>{{cite news |url=https://www.chroniclelive.co.uk/business/business-news/newcastle-company-forefront-technology-small-10869984 |title=Newcastle company at forefront of technology for small nuclear reactors |last=McCusker |first=Peter |website=ChronicleLive.co.uk |location=Newcastle upon Tyne |date=10 February 2016 |accessdate=27 June 2018}}</ref>

His first wife, Hazel, a mathematician, passed away in 2017. They had four sons, all engineers.<ref name=Offshore>[http://www.bwea.com/pdf/Offshoreconf/BWEA_UKOW2006_Programme.pdf Conference Programme] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071009124547/http://www.bwea.com/pdf/Offshoreconf/BWEA_UKOW2006_Programme.pdf |date=9 October 2007 }}, UK Offshore Wind 2006</ref><ref name=FellsAssociates/> In 2018 he married Candida Whitmill, the Managing Director of Penultimate Power UK.

Fells died after a long illness on 20 August 2025, at the age of 92.<ref name="obit"/>

==Honours==
In 1976, Fells was awarded the [[Beilby Medal and Prize]].<ref name="RSC-Beilby">{{cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/Beilby/winners.asp|title=Beilby Medal and Prize Winners|publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|accessdate=3 March 2015}}</ref> He was then elected [[Fellow]]<ref name="List of Fellows">{{cite web|title=List of Fellows|url=http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows|access-date=16 October 2014|archive-date=8 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608094405/http://www.raeng.org.uk/about-us/people-council-committees/the-fellowship/list-of-fellows|url-status=dead}}</ref> of The [[Royal Academy of Engineering]]<ref name="List of Fellows"/> in 1979 and was President of the Institute of Energy (now the [[Energy Institute]]) for 1978-79. In 1993 he received the [[Michael Faraday Prize|Michael Faraday medal and prize]] from the [[Royal Society]], and was elected Fellow of The [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] in 1996. He was awarded the [[Melchett Medal]] of the [[Energy Institute]] in 1999 and the John Collier Medal of the [[Institution of Chemical Engineers]] in the same year. He was awarded a [[Order of the British Empire|CBE]] in June 2000.<ref name=FellsAssociates>{{cite web |url=http://www.fellsassociates.com/ |title=Fells Associates |publisher=Fells Associates |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418154135/http://www.fellsassociates.com/ |archivedate=18 April 2016}}</ref> In the same year, he presented the [[Higginson Lecture]] at [[Durham University]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dur.ac.uk/ecs/ecs_events/higginson/lig_lect_speaker_info/ |title=School of Engineering and Computing Sciences (ECS) : Speakers abridgment - Durham University |access-date=26 August 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130506003435/http://www.dur.ac.uk/ecs/ecs_events/higginson/lig_lect_speaker_info/ |archive-date=6 May 2013}}</ref>
